London’s safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research

London’s safeguarded wharves play a vital role in keeping the capital supplied with the materials and goods it needs, while helping to take freight off congested roads and reduce transport emissions. But with pressure growing to release riverside land for housing and other development, how much wharf capacity will London need in the decades ahead? Commissioned by the Greater London Authority (GLA), this research by Oxford Economics examines the freight handled by London’s safeguarded wharves, identifies the factors driving future demand and forecasts the capacity required to 2050.

Drawing on ten years of freight data from the Port of London Authority, forecasts of industrial demand and interviews with wharf operators, the research provides a detailed picture of how the market could evolve. It examines seven commodity groups, from construction materials and agricultural bulks to metals, petroleum products and waste, and considers how demand will vary across the North East, South East and West regions of the Thames. The findings point to a potential capacity shortfall by 2050, with demand for construction materials alone forecast to exceed available capacity by 622,000 tonnes. The analysis also highlights important differences between regions, suggesting that the location of future capacity could be just as important as its overall level.

The findings have important implications for the future of London’s riverside infrastructure and its ambitions for growth. They highlight the need to consider not just how much wharf capacity the capital requires, but where it is located, which commodities it can handle and how efficiently it is used. The report also explores the uncertainties surrounding future demand and capacity, including the impact of major infrastructure projects, wharf closures and changing river connectivity. Together, the analysis provides an evidence base to inform decisions about the future safeguarding of London’s wharves and the role of the Thames in supporting a growing, more sustainable city.

The experts behind the research

Andy Logan
Director of Industry Consulting

Andy Logan
Director of Industry Consulting

Andy Logan leads our Consultancy offer on different industries for clients. He undertakes studies forecasting the demand for company’s products, analysing the drivers of different industries growth, and assessing the size of different markets and industries. He also investigates the competitive pressures and opportunities facing industries now and in the future. Another area, where he has a keen interest is in studies assessing the demand and supply of labour for different industries and occupations, identifying potential skill shortages and implications for migration.
He has worked with clients in most industries, and in many countries of the world.
Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Andy worked in a variety of economist roles at the Bank of England for 15 years. His research focused on the labour market, commodity and producer prices, UK trade flows, and the performance of UK banks. He holds an MSc. and BA. degrees from the universities of London and Leicester.

Emily Gladstone
Lead Economist

Emily Gladstone
Lead Economist

Emily is a Senior Economist on the Industry team where she supports bespoke industry projects in areas such as renewable energy, construction and insurance. She is also involved in other projects like economic impact studies.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Emily worked for 5 years as a government economist for the UK Civil Service, working in the Department for International Trade (DIT) and the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS). In DIT she worked on assessing the socio-economic impact of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Freeports. She also worked in a crisis covid-19 analytical team, providing supply chain analysis and reporting of critical goods to ministers. In BEIS, she used economic analysis to develop policy positions for manufactured goods for both Free Trade Agreements, the Northern Ireland Protocol and the UK's Global Tariff Schedule. Emily holds a Bsc in Economics from the University of St Andrews.
